items.approach: Walk the array once while keeping a hash map from value to index. For each number, check whether its complement (target - num) has already been seen; if so, return both indices. Otherwise record the current number and continue. This avoids the O(n^2) pair check.
items.gotcha: Insert the current number only after checking for its complement, or you may pair an element with itself (e.g. target 6 with a single 3).

items.approach: Add each number to a hash set. If an insertion fails because the value is already present, a duplicate exists and you can return true immediately. If the loop finishes, every value was distinct.
items.gotcha: Sorting also works in O(1) extra space but costs O(n log n) and mutates the input, so mention the trade-off rather than defaulting to it.

items.approach: All anagrams share the same multiset of letters, so build a canonical key from each word and group words by that key in a hash map. Counting the 26 lowercase letters gives a key in O(k) per word, faster than sorting each word. Return the map's values as the groups.
items.gotcha: An IntArray can't be a map key directly (it uses identity equality), so convert the counts to a String or List with separators so that counts like 1,11 and 11,1 don't collide.

items.approach: Two strings are anagrams exactly when every letter appears the same number of times in each. Use a 26-slot count array: increment for characters of s and decrement for characters of t. If every slot ends at zero, they are anagrams. Bail out early if the lengths differ.
items.gotcha: Forgetting the length check lets strings like "a" and "ab" slip through if you only iterate over one of them.

items.approach: Count frequencies with a hash map, then bucket the numbers by frequency: bucket[f] holds every number that appears f times. A frequency can be at most n, so there are n+1 buckets. Walk the buckets from highest frequency down, collecting numbers until you have k. This beats sorting by frequency.
items.gotcha: Sizing the bucket array as n instead of n+1 crashes when every element is the same value (frequency n).

items.approach: The answer at i is the product of everything to its left times everything to its right. First fill the output with prefix products in a left-to-right pass, then sweep right-to-left with a running suffix product and multiply it in. No division is needed, so zeros are handled naturally.
items.gotcha: Using total product divided by nums[i] breaks when the array contains a zero (and division is disallowed anyway).

items.approach: Scan prices once, tracking the lowest price seen so far. At each day, the best sale today is price minus that minimum; keep the maximum of these. Buying must happen before selling, which the single left-to-right pass guarantees.
items.gotcha: Taking global max minus global min ignores ordering; if the max comes before the min the answer should be 0, not negative or wrong.

items.approach: Put every number in a hash set. A number starts a sequence only if num - 1 is not in the set; from each such start, count upward while num + 1 exists. Each element is visited by at most one upward walk, so the total work is linear.
items.gotcha: Starting a walk from every number (not just sequence starts) degrades to O(n^2), and iterating the raw array instead of the set repeats work for duplicates.

items.approach: Validate each filled cell against three constraints at once: its row, its column and its 3x3 box. Keep a seen-flag table for each of the 9 rows, 9 columns and 9 boxes, with box index (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3. If a digit is already flagged in any of the three, the board is invalid. The board is fixed at 9x9, so this is constant work.
items.gotcha: The task only checks the filled cells for rule violations; it does not ask whether the puzzle is solvable, so don't try to solve it.

items.approach: Precompute a prefix-sum array where prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements. Any range sum left..right is then prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left], answered in constant time. Using one extra leading zero avoids special-casing left = 0.
items.gotcha: Off-by-one: with a size n+1 prefix array the answer is prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left], not prefix[right] - prefix[left].

items.approach: A subarray i..j sums to k when prefix[j] - prefix[i-1] = k, i.e. some earlier prefix equals current - k. Keep a running prefix sum and a map counting how many times each prefix value has occurred, seeded with {0: 1} for subarrays starting at index 0. Add map[current - k] to the answer at each step. Negative numbers rule out a sliding window, which is why this hash approach is needed.
items.gotcha: Forgetting to seed the map with prefix 0 -> 1 misses every valid subarray that starts at index 0.

items.approach: If two prefix sums have the same remainder mod k, the subarray between them sums to a multiple of k. Store the first index where each remainder appears, seeded with remainder 0 at index -1. When a remainder repeats and the distance from its first index is at least 2, return true. Keeping only the earliest index maximizes the length.
items.gotcha: Overwriting the stored index on each repeat (instead of keeping the first) can make a valid length-2+ subarray look too short, e.g. [0, 0] with any k.

items.approach: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter. When the counter is zero, adopt the current element as candidate; then add one if the element matches the candidate and subtract one otherwise. Because the majority appears more than n/2 times, it cannot be fully cancelled and survives as the final candidate.
items.gotcha: The vote only works because a majority is guaranteed; without that guarantee you'd need a second pass to verify the candidate.

items.approach: Dutch National Flag partitioning with three pointers: everything before low is 0, everything after high is 2, and mid scans the unknown middle. A 0 is swapped to low (advance both low and mid), a 2 is swapped to high (shrink high but do not advance mid), and a 1 just advances mid. One pass sorts the array in place.
items.gotcha: Advancing mid after swapping with high is a bug: the element just swapped in from the end hasn't been examined yet.

items.approach: Kadane's algorithm: at each index, the best subarray ending here either extends the previous best ending or starts fresh at this element, so current = max(num, current + num). Track the overall maximum of current across the array. Starting from the first element handles all-negative arrays correctly.
items.gotcha: Initializing best to 0 returns 0 for an all-negative array like [-3, -1], but the answer must be -1 since the subarray can't be empty.
